transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-22
Time: 15:00 - 16:05 UTC
Duration: ~65 minutes
Attendees: Alex Romero (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marcus Li (Redwood SA); Tom Hastings (CISO, Gateway TrustBank), Lena Ortiz (Head of Infra), David Park (Lead Cloud Engineer), Monique Reid (Compliance)

Auto-summary: Security deep-dive focused on private VPC deployment. Conversation mixes architecture diagrams, firewall/NACL discussion, KMS integration, and compliance mapping. A few transcription artifacts; speaker overlaps at times.

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — I'm Alex, AE on the account, with Priya and Marcus from our solutions team. Tom, do you want to start with a quick goal for today?
[00:12] Tom (CISO): Sure. We want to validate that Redwood's Private offering can meet our network isolation and compliance needs — SOC2 controls, auditability, data residency, and that we can lock down ingress/egress. Also looking at options for on-prem or air-gapped if needed.
[00:25] Priya (Redwood SE): Great. We'll run through a VPC architecture sketch, talk about ingress egress patterns, firewalling, and then cover KMS, logging, and auth. Please interrupt if you wanna dive deeper.
[00:35] Lena (Infra): Our current infra is multi-account on LargeCloud, private VPCs per environment, default NAT for egress. We prefer not to open any public inbound endpoints; private endpoints or NGW is better.
[00:48] David (Cloud Eng): Also want to confirm that instance metadata and open IAM metadata endpoints will be controlled — we have strict policies for IMDS v2 only.
[00:55] Priya: Absolutely. On our Private deployment we support placement inside customer VPCs with either VPC peering, PrivateLink-style endpoints, or running within your account via an appliance. The default pattern Redwood recommends is dedicated subnets for control plane components, and strictly private subnets for runtime nodes with no public IPs.
[01:15] Tom: When you say control plane, is that in Redwood's account or ours?
[01:19] Marcus: Two options. For VPC-mode Private the control plane can be in Redwood-managed control plane with a customer-managed data plane inside your VPC; or full Private where both control and data plane run in your account (we've done this for air-gapped or regulated banks).
[01:33] Tom: Preferable to have the data plane in our account. Control plane in Redwood's may be acceptable if metadata and logs are streamed to our SIEM and we keep keys.
[01:42] Alex: Noted. We'll document both options and highlight which controls are available for each.
[01:48] [02:10] Priya: On ingress, we avoid public load balancers for the runtime. We provide a private endpoint — either via AWS PrivateLink or by deploying an NLB with internal-only scope. For egress, we recommend using NAT gateways with strict egress firewalling, or an egress proxy so you can centralize allowlists. We also support forced tunneling to your on-prem firewall.
[02:35] David: For egress, our security team requires only outbound to specific IP ranges for telemetry and no direct internet access. Can Redwood batch updates or pull model artifacts from S3 in a controlled fashion?
[02:48] Priya: Yes, model artifacts can be pulled from objects you host — we support S3 with VPC endpoints and role-based access. You can also supply artifacts via a private artifact registry that Redwood can reach over VPC peering or a transit gateway.
[03:02] Tom: How about firewall rules and security groups — how fine-grained are they? We need to satisfy segmentation and prevent lateral movement.
[03:10] Marcus: We use security groups for host-level controls and recommend subnet-level NACLs for coarse-grained rules. For example, worker nodes only need to talk to the KV cache/gRPC port and the control plane over TLS. We can lock down admin ports entirely behind a bastion or awsec2 session manager.
[03:30] Lena: Do you have examples of NACLs and SGs?
[03:33] Alex: We'll share a config checklist with example SGs and NACLs — that's one of the action items.
[03:36] [04:00] Monique (Compliance): Quick interjection — we need end-to-end encryption at rest and in transit, key ownership clarity, and auditability. SOC2 focus is on how keys are managed and whether Redwood can access plaintext.
[04:14] Priya: By default data is encrypted at rest using customer-managed KMS keys if requested. We can integrate with your KMS or use a Redwood-managed key. For highest assurance, we recommend customer-managed KMS with key policies that restrict root or service access. We also support HSM-backed keys for stricter controls.
[04:36] Tom: If we use our KMS, do you need key access for routine operations like model loading?
[04:42] Marcus: We only require decrypt permission for the service principal running in the data plane to load model weights. All requests are logged. You can use separate keys per environment and rotate them.
[04:51] [05:15] David: On logging — we need all admin operations, API calls, and model access events sent to our centralized SIEM with 365-day retention. Any PII redaction?
[05:25] Priya: We stream audit logs and usage events to your CloudWatch/Logging endpoint or via syslog/S3. We can redact or hash sensitive tokens before shipping. Retention is configurable; for SOC2 we usually suggest 1 year, ISO could be different — we'll map those controls.
[05:42] Monique: Good. Make sure the audit trail includes who requested model versions, who created API keys, and any privileged role changes.
[05:50] Alex: We have role-based audit entries — we'll include a sample log schema in the doc packet.
[05:55] [07:00] Tom: Network IDS/IPS — do you integrate with existing IDS or provide support for traffic mirroring?
[07:07] Marcus: Yes, we can configure VPC traffic mirroring to your IDS appliances. Alternatively you can run inline proxies. We support flow logs and will provide packet metadata if you need deeper inspection.
[07:22] Lena: About ingress certificates — do you support mutual TLS between the control plane and data plane?
[07:29] Priya: Yes. We use mTLS for all control plane to node communications. Certificates can be managed by Redwood or you can provide your own CA for issuing node certs. For internal-only LB we recommend MTLS.
[07:42] [08:10] David: For on-prem or air-gapped, what does provisioning look like? We sometimes need a fully offline runtime.
[08:17] Marcus: For air-gapped, we deliver a deployable appliance (container/VM images) and an ops runbook. Initial provisioning may require a one-time transfer of artifacts (air-gapped USB or secure transfer). After that, everything runs on-premises — control and data plane can both be installed if required. There are operational tradeoffs: updates are slower and we rely on your patching cadence.
[08:40] Tom: Do you support hardware attestation or secure boot?
[08:44] Priya: We can integrate with HSMs and support attestation if your hardware supports it. Secure boot is customer-managed; we provide guidance.
[08:53] [09:30] Monique: For compliance mapping — can you provide a SOC2 artifact package?
[09:35] Alex: Yes, we have a SOC2 report, ISO 27001 summary, and an architecture checklist we can share. For Private deployments we provide a different artifact with design docs and controls we expect to be customer-owned.
[09:50] Monique: Also need SSO/SAML integration and RBAC for admin UI.
[09:56] Priya: Redwood supports SAML SSO, OIDC, and SCIM for user provisioning. RBAC is granular — roles for admin, deploy, read-only, billing. We also support service principals with limited scopes for automation.
[10:10] David: Any protections for preventing token exfiltration from the nodes?
[10:15] Marcus: We recommend ephemeral credentials and instance profiles with minimal privileges; disable metadata service where possible, or enforce v2 only. Additionally, we can inject secrets at runtime from KMS and avoid writing secrets to disk.
[10:29] [11:00] Lena: How about egress filtering at network layer vs application layer — which do you recommend?
[11:05] Priya: Defense in depth. Start with strict NACLs and SG egress allowlists, then add application-level proxies that validate destination domains and SNI. For telemetry, use a dedicated egress IP range so your IDS can monitor.
[11:22] Tom: What about DLP — preventing model outputs from leaking sensitive customer data?
[11:28] Priya: We offer content filtering and can set data loss prevention patterns at the prompt layer. For higher assurance, run the model in your private VPC and restrict training/ingestion pipelines.
[11:40] [12:30] David: We have regulators that require egress via our Palo Alto firewall and log retention in our Splunk. Can Redwood forward logs to Splunk?
[12:36] Priya: Yes — we support syslog, Kinesis, direct CloudWatch -> Splunk, and S3 ingestion. We'll include sample configs.
[12:46] Monique: Is there a feature to redact PII before logs leave the VPC?
[12:50] Priya: Yes, we can perform inline redaction or hashing before streaming. That configuration is per environment.
[13:00] [14:00] Alex: Quick note on rollout strategy — for Dedicated + Private pilot we usually do a canary in a non-prod VPC, run throughput tests, then expand to prod VPC once controls are satisfied.
[14:12] Tom: Can you run a perf test with our model payloads to validate that the egress and peering don't add unacceptable latency?
[14:18] Marcus: Yes — that's part of the pilot. We'll coordinate with David to get sample payloads and routes.
[14:26] [15:00] David: One more question — how are software updates handled in Private mode?
[15:04] Priya: Updates are controlled. For fully customer-hosted deployments, you trigger upgrades on your cadence; we provide patched images and CVE notes. For Redwood-managed data plane within your VPC, we can schedule maintenance windows and provide hotpatch or rolling updates.
[15:20] Tom: Any SLA impact for air-gapped?
[15:24] Alex: SLA is different — air-gapped deployments have operational constraints so we negotiate support terms. We'll document expected MTTR.
[15:35] [16:10] Monique: Final — please include how RBAC map to logs and change control evidence for SOC2.
[16:16] Alex: We'll include a mapping matrix: control -> evidence -> artifact.
[16:22] Priya: We'll also send example firewall rules, mTLS cert rotation cadence, and KMS key policy templates.
[16:30] Tom: Great. Sounds like a plan.
[16:35] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the doc pack and schedule the network walkthrough.

End transcript. Some minor transcription artifacts present (speaker overlaps, a few garbled words).
